stimuli.title: Reading comprehension: passage 1
stimuli.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

India grows more fruit and vegetables than almost any other country, yet a large share never reaches a plate. Tomatoes split in the heat of a truck, bananas ripen too fast in an open godown, and peas lose their sweetness long before they reach a market a few hundred kilometres away. The loss is counted in rupees, but it is also counted in the water, fertiliser and labour that went into growing food nobody eats.

The usual answer is a cold chain: a series of cooled spaces that carries produce from the field to the shop without a break. The weak link is rarely the large cold store in the city. It is the first mile, the hours between picking and the first cool room, when the produce is still warm from the field and most of the damage is done.

Small pack-houses near the farm, where crops are washed, sorted and pre-cooled, address exactly this gap. Some run on solar power and are owned by farmer producer organisations, so that the members share the cost. Farmers who use them report that they can wait for a better price instead of selling the same evening at whatever the trader offers.

The obstacle is less the machinery than its use through the year. A pack-house built for a single crop sits idle for months, and its owners struggle to repay the loan. Planners now favour units that can handle several crops in turn, so that the cooling never stops paying for itself.

stimuli.title: Reading comprehension: passage 2
stimuli.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

For most of history, the question of how to pay for old age was answered by the family. Parents looked after their children, and children, in turn, looked after their parents. That arrangement is changing in India. Families are smaller, young people move to distant cities for work, and people live many years longer than their grandparents did.

Only a minority of workers, mostly in government or large companies, can count on a regular pension. The rest, including shopkeepers, farm workers and the self-employed, must save for themselves, and many do not start until they are well into middle age. By then, the power of compounding, which turns small, early savings into a large sum over decades, has had too little time to work.

Several government-backed schemes now allow even a small monthly contribution, and digital payments have made it easier to keep paying without a trip to a branch. Yet enrolment is one thing and staying enrolled is another. A household that loses a month's income often stops contributing and never restarts.

Researchers suggest a modest change in design: make the next payment automatic unless the saver chooses to stop. People tend to stick with whatever happens by default, and a habit that needs no fresh decision each month is far more likely to survive a difficult year.

stimuli.title: Reading comprehension: passage 1
stimuli.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

Along parts of India's eastern coast, villages that sit behind a belt of mangrove forest have often come through cyclones better than villages a short distance away that have none. The trees do not stop a storm, but their tangled roots slow the water that a cyclone pushes onto the land, and the forest takes the first blow of the wind.

For decades, mangroves were treated as wasteland. They were cleared for fish and shrimp ponds, for salt pans and for new roads and houses. The ponds earned money quickly, but many were abandoned after a few years when disease struck or the soil turned too salty, leaving neither forest nor farm.

Replanting has since become popular, and some projects have done well. Others have planted a single fast-growing species in neat rows on mudflats where mangroves never grew naturally, and most of the saplings died. Experts say the more reliable approach is to restore the flow of tidal water to areas where mangroves once stood, and let the forest return largely by itself.

The forests also support local livelihoods. Crabs, fish and honey from healthy mangroves provide income year after year, which gives villagers a reason to protect the forest long after a planting project has ended.

stimuli.title: Reading comprehension: passage 2
stimuli.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

Each year, millions of young Indians finish school or college and go looking for work, and employers in many industries still say they cannot find people with the right skills. The two complaints sound contradictory, but they point to the same gap: what is learnt in a classroom is often not what is needed on a factory floor or in a hospital ward.

Apprenticeships try to close that gap by letting a young person learn on the job while earning a stipend. The trainee works under an experienced employee, and the classroom part of the course is tied to tasks the trainee actually does. In countries where such training is common, a large share of apprentices are hired by the firm that trained them.

In India the numbers have grown, but they remain small for an economy of its size. Many smaller firms see apprentices as a cost rather than an investment, and fear that a worker they train will simply leave for a better offer. Large companies find the paperwork easier to manage.

Supporters argue that the fear of losing trained workers is overstated. A trainee who has learnt the firm's own machines and methods is often more valuable to it than to anyone else, and many stay for that reason.

stimuli.title: Short passage
stimuli.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

In many villages the nearest bank branch is a bus ride away, and a day's wages can be lost just to deposit a small sum. Business correspondents help to fill this gap. They are local agents, often running a small shop, who open accounts, accept deposits and pay out withdrawals on behalf of a bank using a hand-held device.

The model works best where the agent is trusted and earns enough to stay in business. Where commissions are thin, agents tend to drift away to other work, and customers who had begun to save are left without a nearby point of service. Some banks now pay agents a small fixed amount each month as well as a commission, so that a quiet month does not drive them out.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Solar power should run every cold store across India
City cold stores are the weakest link in the whole chain
Much produce spoils early, and cooling near the farm helps
Farmers should always sell their crops on the day of harvest
India grows too little fruit to feed its own people
questions.explanation: The passage says most damage happens in the first mile and that pack-houses near the farm address that gap. It says India grows more produce than almost any country, and that the city cold store is rarely the weak link.

questions.stem: According to the passage, where is the weak link in the cold chain?
options: The trucks that carry produce between states
The first hours between picking and cooling
The markets where traders set the price
The shops that sell produce to customers
The large cold stores in the cities
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the weak link is rarely the city cold store but the first mile, the hours between picking and the first cool room.

questions.stem: Why can farmers who use pack-houses get a better price?
options: They can store produce and wait to sell
Their crops grow faster after cooling
Their produce is sent straight abroad
The pack-house buys all their crops
Traders are required to pay them more
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says farmers can wait for a better price instead of selling the same evening at whatever the trader offers, which they can do only because the produce keeps.

questions.stem: What problem does the passage identify with pack-houses built for a single crop?
options: They are too far away from the farms
They stand unused for much of the year
They damage the crops they are cooling
They cannot be run on solar power
They are too small for a whole village
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says a pack-house built for one crop sits idle for months and its owners struggle to repay the loan.

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly the SAME in meaning as 'favour' as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: 'Planners now favour units that can handle several crops' means they prefer such units. 'Reward' is another sense of favour that does not fit here.

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to 'idle' as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: An idle pack-house is unused; the opposite is busy. Empty, quiet and closed are close to idle in meaning.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

Why Young People Move to the Cities

questions.explanation: The passage moves from the family's old role to the need for workers to save for themselves and how to keep them saving. The other titles pick out a single detail or something the passage does not say.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which workers can usually count on a regular pension?

questions.explanation: I: x = 9 or −9. II: (y + 9)² = 0, so y = −9. x = 9 is greater than −9 and x = −9 equals it, so x ≥ y.

questions.stem: What were the total fixed deposits (in ₹ lakh) of all five branches in Quarter 2?
By what percentage did branch M's deposits rise from Quarter 1 to Quarter 2?
questions.explanation: M rose from 180 to 234, an increase of 54. 54 ÷ 180 = 0.3, so 30%.

questions.stem: What is the ratio of branch L's deposits in Quarter 1 to branch O's deposits in Quarter 2?
questions.explanation: 320 : 138. Dividing both by 2 gives 160 : 69.

questions.stem: What were the average Quarter 1 deposits (in ₹ lakh) of branches K, M, N and O?
How many books did the four shops sell online in all?
The books shop Y sold in the shop (not online) are what percentage more than the books shop X sold in the shop?
questions.explanation: Y sold 60% of 900 = 540 in the shop and X sold 75% of 640 = 480. 60 more on 480 is 12.5%.

questions.stem: What is the ratio of the books sold online by shop W to those sold online by shop Z?
questions.explanation: W sold 35% of 800 = 280 online and Z sold 50% of 560 = 280 online, so the ratio is 1 : 1.

questions.stem: Next month shop X sells the same total number of books, but its online sales rise by 50%. What percentage of its books are then sold online?
questions.explanation: X sold 25% of 640 = 160 online. A 50% rise gives 240, and 240 ÷ 640 = 37.5%. Adding 50% to the 25% share itself would wrongly give 75%.

questions.stem: A trader marks a mixer grinder 50% above its cost price and then allows a discount of 20%. What is his profit percentage?
questions.explanation: On a cost of 100 the marked price is 150, and 20% off leaves 120. The profit is 20%. Subtracting 20 from 50 would wrongly give 30%.

questions.stem: A sum of money earns simple interest of ₹2,880 in 3 years at 8% per annum. What is the sum?
questions.explanation: Interest for 3 years at 8% is 24% of the sum. 2,880 ÷ 0.24 = 12,000.

questions.stem: The difference between the compound interest and the simple interest on a sum for 2 years at 8% per annum, compounded annually, is ₹64. What is the sum?
questions.explanation: For 2 years the difference is P × (r/100)², so P × 0.0064 = 64 and P = 10,000.

questions.stem: A can finish a piece of work in 15 days and B in 20 days. They work together for 6 days, and then A leaves. In how many days will B finish the remaining work?
questions.explanation: Together they do 1/15 + 1/20 = 7/60 a day, so 42/60 = 7/10 in 6 days. B does the remaining 3/10 at 1/20 a day, which takes 6 days.

questions.stem: A goods train 450 m long crosses a pole in 27 seconds. What is its speed in km/h?
A motorboat's speed in still water is 20 km/h and the river flows at 4 km/h. How many hours will it take to go 48 km downstream and return to the start?
questions.explanation: Downstream speed is 24 km/h (2 hours) and upstream 16 km/h (3 hours), so 5 hours in all. Ignoring the current gives 4.8 hours.

questions.stem: The present ages of A and B are in the ratio 5 : 7. After 6 years the ratio will be 3 : 4. What is B's present age in years?
questions.explanation: Let the ages be 5x and 7x. (5x + 6) : (7x + 6) = 3 : 4 gives 20x + 24 = 21x + 18, so x = 6 and B is 42.

questions.stem: 60 litres of a mixture contain milk and water in the ratio 7 : 3. How many litres of water must be added to make the ratio 3 : 2?
questions.explanation: Milk is 42 litres and water 18. For 42 : (18 + w) = 3 : 2, 18 + w = 28, so w = 10.

questions.stem: Farah invests ₹35,000 for 12 months and Gopal invests ₹45,000 for 8 months in a business. Out of a profit of ₹39,000, what is Farah's share?
questions.explanation: The shares are in the ratio 35,000 × 12 : 45,000 × 8 = 420 : 360 = 7 : 6. Farah gets 7/13 of 39,000 = 21,000.

questions.stem: A bag holds 5 red, 4 blue and 3 green balls. Two balls are drawn at random together. What is the probability that both are blue?
questions.explanation: There are 4C2 = 6 ways to pick two blue balls out of 12C2 = 66 ways in all, so 6/66 = 1/11.

questions.stem:
A statement is followed by two conclusions, I and II. Assume the statement is true and decide which conclusion(s) definitely follow.

Statement: B ≤ C < D = E ≥ F

I. B < E

II. F ≤ D
questions.explanation: I: B ≤ C < D = E gives B < E, true. II: D = E ≥ F gives D ≥ F, which is the same as F ≤ D, true. Both follow.

questions.stem:
A statement is followed by two conclusions, I and II. Assume the statement is true and decide which conclusion(s) definitely follow.

Statement: G > H ≥ I ≤ J < K

I. G > I

II. K > H
questions.explanation: I: G > H ≥ I gives G > I, true. II: H ≥ I and I ≤ J point in opposite directions, so H and K cannot be compared. Only I follows.

questions.stem:
A statement is followed by two conclusions, I and II. Assume the statement is true and decide which conclusion(s) definitely follow.

Statement: P ≥ Q = R ≤ S

I. P > R

II. P = R
questions.explanation: P ≥ Q = R, so P ≥ R. Neither 'P > R' nor 'P = R' is certain on its own, but one of them must be true. Either I or II follows.

questions.stem:
Some statements are followed by two conclusions, I and II. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to differ from commonly known facts, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow.

Statements: All pens are clips. Some clips are pins.

I. Some pens are pins.

II. Some pins are clips.
questions.explanation: The pins that are clips need not be the clips that are pens, so I is only a possibility. 'Some clips are pins' converts to 'Some pins are clips', so II follows. Only II follows.

questions.stem:
Some statements are followed by two conclusions, I and II. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to differ from commonly known facts, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow.

Statements: No rose is a lily. All lilies are tulips.

I. Some tulips are not roses.

II. All roses are tulips.
questions.explanation: The tulips that are lilies cannot be roses, so some tulips are not roses (I). Nothing says roses are tulips, so II does not follow. Only I follows.

questions.stem:
Some statements are followed by two conclusions, I and II. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to differ from commonly known facts, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow.

Statements: Some tickets are coupons. No coupon is a receipt.

I. Some tickets are not receipts.

II. No ticket is a receipt.
questions.explanation: The tickets that are coupons cannot be receipts, so some tickets are not receipts (I). Other tickets may still be receipts, so II is not certain. Only I follows.

questions.stem: Who lives on floor 5?
questions.explanation: Floors 1 to 7: K (Audit), P (Legal), M (IT), R (Loans), T (HR), L (Sales), N (Treasury). R is on 4, so Treasury is on 1 or 7; N is above R, so N is on 7 and L on 6. Audit is on 1 and P on 2. M is below R and two floors from K, with K lower, so K is on 1 and M on 3, leaving T on 5, the HR floor. L is not Loans, so L is Sales and R Loans. T is on floor 5.

questions.stem: In which department does R work?
questions.explanation: Floors 1 to 7: K (Audit), P (Legal), M (IT), R (Loans), T (HR), L (Sales), N (Treasury). R is on 4, so Treasury is on 1 or 7; N is above R, so N is on 7 and L on 6. Audit is on 1 and P on 2. M is below R and two floors from K, with K lower, so K is on 1 and M on 3, leaving T on 5, the HR floor. L is not Loans, so L is Sales and R Loans.

questions.stem: How many persons live between K and L?
questions.explanation: Floors 1 to 7: K (Audit), P (Legal), M (IT), R (Loans), T (HR), L (Sales), N (Treasury). R is on 4, so Treasury is on 1 or 7; N is above R, so N is on 7 and L on 6. Audit is on 1 and P on 2. M is below R and two floors from K, with K lower, so K is on 1 and M on 3, leaving T on 5, the HR floor. L is not Loans, so L is Sales and R Loans. questions.stem: Who lives immediately above the person who works in IT?

IT is M on floor 3, and R is on floor 4.

questions.stem: Which of the following combinations is correct?
questions.explanation: Floors 1 to 7: K (Audit), P (Legal), M (IT), R (Loans), T (HR), L (Sales), N (Treasury). R is on 4, so Treasury is on 1 or 7; N is above R, so N is on 7 and L on 6. Audit is on 1 and P on 2. M is below R and two floors from K, with K lower, so K is on 1 and M on 3, leaving T on 5, the HR floor. L is not Loans, so L is Sales and R Loans.

questions.stem: Who sits opposite F?
questions.explanation: Clockwise from A (facing the centre, a person's left is the next seat clockwise): A, F, C, H, E, B, G, D. C is second to A's left and F between them; E is opposite A and H on E's right; D is on A's right, B second to D's right, and G takes the last seat. F is in the 2nd seat and B four seats on, in the 6th.

questions.stem: Who sits immediately to the left of G?
questions.explanation: Clockwise from A (facing the centre, a person's left is the next seat clockwise): A, F, C, H, E, B, G, D. C is second to A's left and F between them; E is opposite A and H on E's right; D is on A's right, B second to D's right, and G takes the last seat. The next seat clockwise from G is D.

questions.stem: Counting clockwise from C, how many persons sit between C and B?
questions.explanation: Clockwise from A (facing the centre, a person's left is the next seat clockwise): A, F, C, H, E, B, G, D. C is second to A's left and F between them; E is opposite A and H on E's right; D is on A's right, B second to D's right, and G takes the last seat. Clockwise from C: H, E, then B.

questions.stem: Who sits third to the left of E?
questions.explanation: Clockwise from A (facing the centre, a person's left is the next seat clockwise): A, F, C, H, E, B, G, D. C is second to A's left and F between them; E is opposite A and H on E's right; D is on A's right, B second to D's right, and G takes the last seat. Clockwise from E: B, G, D. D is third to the left.

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs sit next to each other?
questions.explanation: Clockwise from A (facing the centre, a person's left is the next seat clockwise): A, F, C, H, E, B, G, D. C is second to A's left and F between them; E is opposite A and H on E's right; D is on A's right, B second to D's right, and G takes the last seat.

questions.stem: Who goes to Kochi?
questions.explanation: In month order: Q (January, Kochi), T (March, Pune), P (April, Shimla), U (June, Delhi), R (September, Ranchi), S (November, Bhopal). S is last, so P is third, in April. Kochi is first and T second. U and R are consecutive in the free months, June and September, which leaves January to Q. P takes Shimla, and T, not Delhi, takes Pune.

questions.stem: In which month does U attend?
questions.explanation: In month order: Q (January, Kochi), T (March, Pune), P (April, Shimla), U (June, Delhi), R (September, Ranchi), S (November, Bhopal). S is last, so P is third, in April. Kochi is first and T second. U and R are consecutive in the free months, June and September, which leaves January to Q. P takes Shimla, and T, not Delhi, takes Pune.

questions.stem: How many persons attend between T and R?
questions.explanation: In month order: Q (January, Kochi), T (March, Pune), P (April, Shimla), U (June, Delhi), R (September, Ranchi), S (November, Bhopal). S is last, so P is third, in April. Kochi is first and T second. U and R are consecutive in the free months, June and September, which leaves January to Q. P takes Shimla, and T, not Delhi, takes Pune. P (April) and U (June) attend between T (March) and R (September).

questions.stem: To which city does the person who attends in September go?
questions.explanation: In month order: Q (January, Kochi), T (March, Pune), P (April, Shimla), U (June, Delhi), R (September, Ranchi), S (November, Bhopal). S is last, so P is third, in April. Kochi is first and T second. U and R are consecutive in the free months, June and September, which leaves January to Q. P takes Shimla, and T, not Delhi, takes Pune.

questions.stem: Who attends immediately before S?
questions.explanation: In month order: Q (January, Kochi), T (March, Pune), P (April, Shimla), U (June, Delhi), R (September, Ranchi), S (November, Bhopal). S is last, so P is third, in April. Kochi is first and T second. U and R are consecutive in the free months, June and September, which leaves January to Q. P takes Shimla, and T, not Delhi, takes Pune.

questions.stem: In a certain code, 'DEBT' is written as 'EFCU'. How is 'FUND' written in that code?
questions.explanation: Each letter moves one place forward: D→E, E→F, B→C, T→U. So F→G, U→V, N→O, D→E, giving GVOE.

questions.stem: In a certain code, 'SAFE' is written as 'FGBT'. How is 'CASH' written in that code?
questions.explanation: The word is reversed (SAFE → EFAS) and each letter moves one place forward (E→F, F→G, A→B, S→T). CASH reversed is HSAC, which becomes ITBD.

questions.stem: In a certain code language, 'gold coin bank' is written as 'ta ri mo', 'coin is safe' as 'ri pe lu' and 'safe gold rate' as 'lu ta zi'. What is the code for 'bank'?
questions.explanation: 'gold' is common to the first and third sentences, so gold = ta. 'coin' is common to the first and second, so coin = ri. That leaves bank = mo.

questions.stem: Pointing to a boy, Kavita said, 'He is the son of the only brother of my husband.' How is the boy related to Kavita?
questions.explanation: The only brother of Kavita's husband is her brother-in-law, and his son is her nephew.

questions.stem: A is the sister of B. B is the father of C, who is a boy. D is the mother of A. How is C related to D?
questions.explanation: D is the mother of A and so of A's brother B. C is B's son, so C is D's grandson.

questions.stem: Ravi walks 10 m north, turns right and walks 9 m, turns right and walks 22 m, then turns left and walks 7 m. How far and in which direction is he from his starting point?
questions.explanation: He ends 9 + 7 = 16 m east and 22 − 10 = 12 m south of the start. The distance is √(16² + 12²) = 20 m, towards the south-east.

questions.stem: Meera is facing west. She turns 90° clockwise and then 135° anticlockwise. Which direction is she facing now?
questions.explanation: From west, 90° clockwise is north. From north, 90° anticlockwise is west and 45° more is south-west.

questions.stem: In a row of 45 students, Kavya is 16th from the left end and Mohit is 20th from the right end. How many students sit between them?
questions.explanation: Mohit is 45 − 20 + 1 = 26th from the left. Between the 16th and 26th places there are 26 − 16 − 1 = 9 students.

questions.stem: If the English alphabet is written in reverse order, from Z to A, which letter is 7th to the left of the 21st letter from the left?
questions.explanation: In reverse order the 21st letter from the left is F, and 7th to its left is the 14th letter in the reversed list, which is M (Z is 1st, so the 14th is the 13th letter of the alphabet).

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Mangroves shield coasts and regrow best when tides return
Mangroves can stop a cyclone from reaching the coast
Planting saplings in neat rows is the surest way to restore forests
Shrimp ponds are the most profitable use of coastal land
Villagers should leave the coast before every cyclone
questions.explanation: The passage explains how mangroves reduce cyclone damage and says restoring tidal flow works better than planting in rows. It says plainly that the trees do not stop a storm.

questions.stem: How do mangroves reduce the damage done by a cyclone?
options: They turn the wind away from the villages
They absorb all the rain that falls
They lower the level of the sea all year
Their roots slow the water pushed inland
They stop the storm before it reaches land
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the roots slow the water a cyclone pushes onto the land and the forest takes the first blow of the wind. It says the trees do not stop a storm.

questions.stem: What happened to many of the ponds dug where mangroves were cleared?
options: They were turned into salt pans
They were sold to build new roads
They earned money for many decades
They were abandoned after a few years
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says many ponds were abandoned after a few years when disease struck or the soil turned too salty.

questions.stem: Why did most saplings in some replanting projects die?
options: Villagers cut them down for firewood
They were planted where mangroves never grew
They were planted too late in the season
Cyclones washed them away each year
They were planted too far apart
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says some projects planted one species in rows on mudflats where mangroves never grew naturally, and most saplings died.

questions.stem: According to the last paragraph, what gives villagers a reason to protect healthy mangroves?
options: Planting projects pay them to guard it
Officials watch over the forest for them
They fear fines from the government
The law forbids any use of the forest
The forest gives them income every year
questions.explanation: Crabs, fish and honey give income year after year, which gives villagers a reason to protect the forest after a project ends.

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to 'abandoned' as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: An abandoned pond is left behind and given up; a maintained one is kept up. Deserted means nearly the same as abandoned.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How schools should teach factory skills
Using apprenticeships to close a skills gap
Why graduates refuse to work in factories
How hospitals train their own nurses
Why large firms avoid hiring young people
questions.explanation: The passage describes the gap between classroom learning and job needs and how apprenticeships can close it, along with the obstacles in India.

questions.stem: What gap do the two complaints in the first paragraph point to?
options: Classroom learning does not match job needs
Young people dislike work in factories
There are far too few jobs for graduates
Employers pay young workers too little
Colleges admit far too many students
questions.explanation: The writer says what is learnt in a classroom is often not what is needed on a factory floor or in a hospital ward.

questions.stem: How does an apprenticeship differ from ordinary classroom training, according to the passage?
options: The trainee pays a fee to the employer
The trainee skips the classroom entirely
The trainee learns on the job for a stipend
The trainee studies only in the evenings
The trainee works without any guidance
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the young person learns on the job while earning a stipend, under an experienced employee, with the classroom part tied to the job.

questions.stem: Why do many smaller firms hesitate to take apprentices?
options: Apprentices must be hired for life
They may not legally pay a stipend
The training lasts too many years
They have no machines to train on
They fear trained workers will leave
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says smaller firms see apprentices as a cost and fear a worker they train will leave for a better offer.

questions.stem: What is the supporters' main argument in the last paragraph?
options: Most apprentices go to work abroad
Trained workers rarely want better pay
Small firms should not train anyone
Paperwork is no burden for any firm
Skills tied to one firm make workers stay
questions.explanation: Supporters say a trainee who has learnt the firm's own machines and methods is worth more to it than to anyone else, so many stay.

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly the SAME in meaning as 'overstated' as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: A fear that is overstated is made to seem bigger than it is, that is, exaggerated.

questions.stem: Which sentence comes FIRST after rearrangement?
questions.explanation: The correct order is B D E A C F. B describes the families selling to a trader; D says the price was low; E has some decide to bargain as a group; A pools the milk; C says 'the society' could buy a cooling tank; F ends with what the tank achieved.

questions.stem: Which sentence comes SECOND after rearrangement?
questions.explanation: The correct order is B D E A C F. B describes the families selling to a trader; D says the price was low; E has some decide to bargain as a group; A pools the milk; C says 'the society' could buy a cooling tank; F ends with what the tank achieved.

questions.stem: Which sentence comes FOURTH after rearrangement?
questions.explanation: The correct order is B D E A C F. B describes the families selling to a trader; D says the price was low; E has some decide to bargain as a group; A pools the milk; C says 'the society' could buy a cooling tank; F ends with what the tank achieved.

questions.stem: Which sentence comes LAST after rearrangement?
questions.explanation: The correct order is B D E A C F. B describes the families selling to a trader; D says the price was low; E has some decide to bargain as a group; A pools the milk; C says 'the society' could buy a cooling tank; F ends with what the tank achieved.

questions.explanation: The next clause is about polluted air, so the buses give out no fumes on the street.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (2) best?
questions.explanation: Running costs are lower because electric motors need less maintenance than diesel engines.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (3) best?
questions.explanation: Leasing is a way to offset, or balance out, the high price of the bus. Increasing it would make no sense.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (4) best?
questions.explanation: Leasing is contrasted with buying the vehicles outright, that is, paying the full price at once.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (5) best?
questions.explanation: A depot that draws as much power as a small town needs careful planning.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (6) best?
questions.explanation: Without a ready depot the buses cannot be charged, so they stand idle, unused, for weeks.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that fits the blank to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful.

The manager asked the staff to ........ with the new safety rules from Monday.
questions.explanation: One complies with rules. The other words look similar but do not fit 'with the new safety rules'.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that fits the blank to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful.

The village is so ........ that the nearest hospital is three hours away by road.
questions.explanation: A hospital three hours away shows the village is remote, far from towns.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that fits the blank to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful.

He was ........ of the risks, yet he signed the loan papers without reading them.
questions.explanation: 'Yet' signals a contrast: he knew the risks, yet he signed without reading. 'Unaware' removes the contrast, and 'careless of' is not the idiom.

questions.stem:
Choose the pair of words that fits the two blanks, in order, to make the sentence meaningful.

The scheme was ........ last year and has already ........ over a million families.
questions.explanation: A scheme launched last year that has 'already' reached a million families is the only pair that makes sense together.

questions.stem:
Choose the pair of words that fits the two blanks, in order, to make the sentence meaningful.

As the demand for loans ........, the bank had to ........ more staff at its busiest branches.
questions.explanation: Rising demand at the busiest branches means more staff are hired. 'Grown' needs 'had', and falling demand would not call for more staff.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that fits the blank to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful.

The new app makes it ........ for customers to check their balance at any time.
questions.explanation: After 'makes it' the blank needs an adjective: 'makes it convenient for customers'.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence and find the part that contains an error. If there is no error, choose E.

My uncle (A) / gave me an useful (B) / book on banking (C) / for my birthday. (D) / No error (E)
questions.explanation: 'Useful' begins with a 'yoo' sound, which is a consonant sound, so it takes 'a': 'a useful book'.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence and find the part that contains an error. If there is no error, choose E.

The children were (A) / so tired that they (B) / could not hardly walk (C) / back home. (D) / No error (E)
questions.explanation: 'Hardly' is already negative, so 'could not hardly walk' is a double negative. It should be 'could hardly walk back home'.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence and find the part that contains an error. If there is no error, choose E.

Ten kilometres (A) / are a long distance (B) / to walk (C) / every day. (D) / No error (E)
questions.explanation: An amount of distance treated as one quantity takes a singular verb: 'Ten kilometres is a long distance'.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence and find the part that contains an error. If there is no error, choose E.

The scenery of (A) / the hill station (B) / was so beautiful (C) / that we stayed longer. (D) / No error (E)
questions.explanation: The sentence is correct. 'Scenery' is uncountable and takes the singular 'was'.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence and find the part that contains an error. If there is no error, choose E.

Let him and I (A) / finish the report (B) / before the manager (C) / returns. (D) / No error (E)
questions.explanation: 'Let' takes object pronouns: 'Let him and me finish the report'.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence and find the part that contains an error. If there is no error, choose E.

I have seen (A) / that film (B) / last week (C) / with my cousins. (D) / No error (E)
questions.explanation: A finished past time such as 'last week' needs the simple past: 'I saw that film last week'.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence and find the part that contains an error. If there is no error, choose E.

She asked me (A) / where I was going (B) / and why did I (C) / look so worried. (D) / No error (E)
questions.explanation: In reported speech the question takes statement order with no 'did': 'and why I looked so worried'.

questions.stem:
Which of the following should replace the part in bold to make the sentence correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No improvement'.

The doctor advised him **to give up smoking**.
questions.explanation: The sentence is correct: 'advise someone to do something', and 'give up' is followed by the -ing form.

questions.stem:
Which of the following should replace the part in bold to make the sentence correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No improvement'.

**Each of the clerks have** finished the training.
questions.explanation: 'Each' is singular and takes 'has', while 'of the' is followed by the plural 'clerks'.

questions.stem:
Which of the following should replace the part in bold to make the sentence correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No improvement'.

Sunita **married with** a doctor from Pune last year.
questions.explanation: Marry takes a direct object with no preposition: Sunita married a doctor. (She was married to a doctor is also correct, but it describes a state, not the event last year.)

questions.stem:
Which of the following should replace the part in bold to make the sentence correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No improvement'.

The new manager is **more stricter than** the old one.
questions.explanation: 'Stricter' is already comparative, so 'more' is a double comparative. The correct form is 'stricter than'.

questions.stem:
Which of the following should replace the part in bold to make the sentence correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No improvement'.

He **has gone to Delhi yesterday** for a training course.
questions.explanation: 'Yesterday' is a finished past time, so the simple past is needed: 'went to Delhi yesterday'.

questions.stem:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following question?

64% of 750 + 5/6 of 492 = ?
questions.explanation: 64% of 750 = 480 and 5/6 of 492 = 410, so the total is 890.

questions.stem:

1,296 ÷ 36 × 4 − 11² = ?

questions.stem:
Two equations, I and II, are given. Solve both and choose the correct relationship between x and y.

I. x² − 17x + 72 = 0

II. y² − 15y + 56 = 0
options: x = y or no relation can be established

questions.stem:
Two equations, I and II, are given. Solve both and choose the correct relationship between x and y.

I. x² + 7x + 10 = 0

II. y² + 9y + 20 = 0
options: x = y or no relation can be established
questions.explanation: I: x = −2 or −5. II: y = −4 or −5. x = −2 is greater than both, but x = −5 is less than −4. No single relationship holds.

questions.stem:
Two equations, I and II, are given. Solve both and choose the correct relationship between x and y.

I. 3x² + 11x + 6 = 0

II. y² − 4y + 3 = 0
options: x = y or no relation can be established
questions.explanation: I: (3x + 2)(x + 3) = 0, so x = −2/3 or −3. II: (y − 1)(y − 3) = 0, so y = 1 or 3. Both values of x are negative and both values of y positive, so x < y.

questions.stem:
Two equations, I and II, are given. Solve both and choose the correct relationship between x and y.

I. x² − 20x + 99 = 0

II. y² − 13y + 40 = 0
options: x = y or no relation can be established
questions.explanation: I: (x − 9)(x − 11) = 0, so x = 9 or 11. II: y = 5 or 8. Every value of x is greater than every value of y, so x > y.

questions.stem: Which museum had the highest percentage increase in visitors from 2024 to 2025?
questions.explanation: A rose 25%, C 20%, D 30% (27 on 90) and E 15%, while B fell. D had the highest percentage increase.

questions.stem: What was the total number of visitors (in thousands) to all five museums in 2025?
questions.explanation: 150 + 170 + 192 + 117 + 161 = 790 thousand. The 2024 total is 710 thousand.

questions.stem: By what percentage did the number of visitors to museum B fall from 2024 to 2025?
questions.explanation: B fell from 200 to 170, a drop of 30. 30 ÷ 200 = 15%.

questions.stem: What was the average number of visitors (in thousands) to museums A, C and E in 2024?
How many units were rejected by the four factories in all?
The units rejected at F3 are what percentage more than the units rejected at F1?
questions.explanation: F3 rejected 300 and F1 rejected 120. The difference, 180, is 150% of 120.

questions.stem: What is the ratio of units passed at F2 to units passed at F4?
What percentage of the units made at F4 were rejected?
questions.explanation: 2 of every 15 units were rejected, and 2/15 = 13 1/3%.

questions.stem: By selling a cooler for ₹1,330, a trader loses 5%. At what price should he sell it to gain 15%?
What is the compound interest on ₹20,000 for 3 years at 10% per annum, compounded annually?
questions.explanation: The amount is 20,000 × 1.1³ = 26,620, so the interest is 6,620. Simple interest would give 6,000.

questions.stem: 16 workers can lay a pipeline in 21 days. In how many days can 24 workers lay it, working at the same rate?
questions.explanation: The job needs 16 × 21 = 336 worker-days, and 336 ÷ 24 = 14 days.

questions.stem: Pipe A can fill a tank in 12 minutes and pipe B in 18 minutes, while pipe C can empty it in 9 minutes. If all three are opened together on an empty tank, how many minutes will it take to fill?
questions.explanation: Each minute fills 1/12 + 1/18 − 1/9 = (3 + 2 − 4)/36 = 1/36 of the tank, so it fills in 36 minutes.

questions.stem: Two trains 180 m and 240 m long run in opposite directions at 46 km/h and 62 km/h. How many seconds do they take to cross each other?
questions.explanation: The relative speed is 108 km/h = 30 m/s and the distance is 180 + 240 = 420 m, so 420 ÷ 30 = 14 seconds.

questions.stem: The average of six numbers is 35. When one number is removed, the average of the other five is 33. What number was removed?
questions.explanation: The six numbers total 210 and the five left total 165, so the number removed is 45.

questions.stem: Rani's salary is 60% more than Sohan's. By what percentage is Sohan's salary less than Rani's?
questions.explanation: If Sohan earns 100, Rani earns 160. Sohan is 60 less than 160, and 60 ÷ 160 = 37.5%.

questions.stem: ₹7,800 is divided among P, Q and R in the ratio 1/2 : 1/3 : 1/4. What is R's share?
questions.explanation: Multiplying by 12 turns the ratio into 6 : 4 : 3, which has 13 parts. R gets 3/13 of 7,800 = 1,800.

questions.stem: A rectangle is 24 cm long and 18 cm wide. A square has the same perimeter as the rectangle. By how many square centimetres does the square's area exceed the rectangle's?
questions.explanation: The perimeter is 84 cm, so the square's side is 21 cm and its area 441 cm². The rectangle's area is 432 cm², a difference of 9.

questions.stem: Two fair dice are thrown together. What is the probability that the sum of the numbers shown is 9?
questions.explanation: The pairs (3, 6), (4, 5), (5, 4) and (6, 3) give 9: four outcomes out of 36, which is 1/9.

questions.stem:
A statement is followed by two conclusions, I and II. Assume the statement is true and decide which conclusion(s) definitely follow.

Statement: U < V ≤ W = X > Y

I. U < X

II. W > Y
questions.explanation: I: U < V ≤ W = X gives U < X, true. II: W = X > Y gives W > Y, true. Both follow.

questions.stem:
A statement is followed by two conclusions, I and II. Assume the statement is true and decide which conclusion(s) definitely follow.

Statement: M ≥ N > O ≤ P = Q

I. M > O

II. Q ≥ N
questions.explanation: I: M ≥ N > O gives M > O, true. II: N > O and O ≤ P point in opposite directions, so N and Q cannot be compared. Only I follows.

questions.stem:
A statement is followed by two conclusions, I and II. Assume the statement is true and decide which conclusion(s) definitely follow.

Statement: A = B ≥ C > D ≤ E

I. A > E

II. D < B
questions.explanation: I: C > D and D ≤ E point in opposite directions, so A and E cannot be compared. II: B ≥ C > D gives B > D, true. Only II follows.

questions.stem:
Some statements are followed by two conclusions, I and II. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to differ from commonly known facts, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow.

Statements: All trains are buses. All buses are trucks.

I. All trains are trucks.

II. Some trucks are trains.
questions.explanation: Every train is a bus and every bus a truck, so all trains are trucks (I), and so some trucks are trains (II). Both follow.

questions.stem:
Some statements are followed by two conclusions, I and II. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to differ from commonly known facts, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow.

Statements: Some lamps are bulbs. Some bulbs are switches.

I. Some lamps are switches.

II. No lamp is a switch.
questions.explanation: Two 'some' statements give no definite link between lamps and switches. Yet either some lamps are switches or none is, so the pair is complementary. Either I or II follows.

questions.stem:
Some statements are followed by two conclusions, I and II. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to differ from commonly known facts, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow.

Statements: No wall is a door. Some doors are windows.

I. Some windows are walls.

II. All windows are doors.
questions.explanation: Windows and walls are not linked definitely, so I is only a possibility. 'Some doors are windows' does not mean every window is a door. Neither follows.

questions.stem: Who sits second to the right of K?
questions.explanation: Left to right: M, Q, J, O, K, W, L, N. K is 4th from the right, the 5th seat. Q is three seats from K and not at an end, so Q is 2nd and M 1st. N is at the other end with L beside it. O is 4th, and J, not next to K, is 3rd, leaving W 6th.

questions.stem: How many persons sit between M and W?
questions.explanation: Left to right: M, Q, J, O, K, W, L, N. K is 4th from the right, the 5th seat. Q is three seats from K and not at an end, so Q is 2nd and M 1st. N is at the other end with L beside it. O is 4th, and J, not next to K, is 3rd, leaving W 6th. M is 1st and W 6th, so Q, J, O and K sit between them.

questions.stem: Who sits exactly between J and K?
questions.explanation: Left to right: M, Q, J, O, K, W, L, N. K is 4th from the right, the 5th seat. Q is three seats from K and not at an end, so Q is 2nd and M 1st. N is at the other end with L beside it. O is 4th, and J, not next to K, is 3rd, leaving W 6th.

questions.stem: Which pair sits at the two ends of the row?
questions.explanation: Left to right: M, Q, J, O, K, W, L, N. K is 4th from the right, the 5th seat. Q is three seats from K and not at an end, so Q is 2nd and M 1st. N is at the other end with L beside it. O is 4th, and J, not next to K, is 3rd, leaving W 6th.

questions.stem: Who sits second to the left of L?
questions.explanation: Left to right: M, Q, J, O, K, W, L, N. K is 4th from the right, the 5th seat. Q is three seats from K and not at an end, so Q is 2nd and M 1st. N is at the other end with L beside it. O is 4th, and J, not next to K, is 3rd, leaving W 6th. L is 7th, so second to its left is the 5th seat, K.

questions.stem: Who owns the Grey car?
questions.explanation: Floors 1 to 6: Vivek (White), Sana (Red), Zara (Blue), Rohit (Silver), Uday (Black), Tanvi (Grey). Tanvi is on 6, so Blue (Zara) is on 3 and Rohit on 4. Black is on 5. Sana is on the only free even floor, 2, with Vivek below on 1, so Uday is on 5. Red is directly above White: Sana and Vivek. Tanvi has Grey.

questions.stem: On which floor does Uday live?
questions.explanation: Floors 1 to 6: Vivek (White), Sana (Red), Zara (Blue), Rohit (Silver), Uday (Black), Tanvi (Grey). Tanvi is on 6, so Blue (Zara) is on 3 and Rohit on 4. Black is on 5. Sana is on the only free even floor, 2, with Vivek below on 1, so Uday is on 5. Red is directly above White: Sana and Vivek. Tanvi has Grey.

questions.stem: How many persons live between Sana and Uday?
questions.explanation: Floors 1 to 6: Vivek (White), Sana (Red), Zara (Blue), Rohit (Silver), Uday (Black), Tanvi (Grey). Tanvi is on 6, so Blue (Zara) is on 3 and Rohit on 4. Black is on 5. Sana is on the only free even floor, 2, with Vivek below on 1, so Uday is on 5. Red is directly above White: Sana and Vivek. Tanvi has Grey. Zara and Rohit live between floors 2 and 5.

questions.stem: What colour is the car of the person who lives immediately below Rohit?
questions.explanation: Floors 1 to 6: Vivek (White), Sana (Red), Zara (Blue), Rohit (Silver), Uday (Black), Tanvi (Grey). Tanvi is on 6, so Blue (Zara) is on 3 and Rohit on 4. Black is on 5. Sana is on the only free even floor, 2, with Vivek below on 1, so Uday is on 5. Red is directly above White: Sana and Vivek. Tanvi has Grey. Zara lives below Rohit and owns the Blue car.

questions.stem: Who lives immediately above Vivek?
questions.explanation: Floors 1 to 6: Vivek (White), Sana (Red), Zara (Blue), Rohit (Silver), Uday (Black), Tanvi (Grey). Tanvi is on 6, so Blue (Zara) is on 3 and Rohit on 4. Black is on 5. Sana is on the only free even floor, 2, with Vivek below on 1, so Uday is on 5. Red is directly above White: Sana and Vivek. Tanvi has Grey.

questions.stem: Who has the second-highest savings?
questions.explanation: Most to least: H, K, F, J, G, I. I is last and G fifth. K > F > J > G, and H > K, so H is first.

questions.stem: How many persons have less savings than F?
questions.explanation: Most to least: H, K, F, J, G, I. I is last and G fifth. K > F > J > G, and H > K, so H is first. J, G and I have less than F.

questions.stem: Who has the third-lowest savings?
questions.explanation: Most to least: H, K, F, J, G, I. I is last and G fifth. K > F > J > G, and H > K, so H is first. From the bottom: I, G, then J.

questions.stem: Which of the following is definitely true?
options: G has more savings than I
I has more savings than G
J has less savings than G
F has more savings than K
questions.explanation: Most to least: H, K, F, J, G, I. I is last and G fifth. K > F > J > G, and H > K, so H is first.

questions.stem: Who are third and fourth when the savings are arranged from highest to lowest?
questions.explanation: Most to least: H, K, F, J, G, I. I is last and G fifth. K > F > J > G, and H > K, so H is first.

questions.stem: In a certain code, 'PRICE' is written as 'OQHBD'. How is 'STOCK' written in that code?
questions.explanation: Each letter moves one place back: P→O, R→Q, I→H, C→B, E→D. So S→R, T→S, O→N, C→B, K→J, giving RSNBJ.

questions.stem: If 'BAD' is coded as 7 because B = 2, A = 1 and D = 4 are added, how is 'FEED' coded?
In a certain code language, 'loan is easy' is written as 'ka mu so', 'easy to pay' as 'so ri ne' and 'pay the loan' as 'ne ka ti'. What is the code for 'to'?
questions.explanation: easy = so (first and second), loan = ka (first and third) and pay = ne (second and third). The remaining code in the second sentence, ri, is 'to'.

questions.stem: Introducing a woman, Arjun said, 'Her brother's father is my father's father's only son.' How is the woman related to Arjun?
questions.explanation: The only son of Arjun's grandfather is Arjun's father. The woman's brother's father is her own father, so she is a daughter of Arjun's father: Arjun's sister.

questions.stem: P is the brother of Q, who is a girl. R is the wife of P. S is a son of Q's father, but S is not P. How is S related to R?
questions.explanation: S is another son of the same father, so S is P's brother. The brother of R's husband is her brother-in-law.

questions.stem: Sunil walks 15 m south, turns left and walks 8 m, then turns left again and walks 21 m. How far and in which direction is he from his starting point?
questions.explanation: Turning left from south faces east, and left again faces north. He ends 8 m east and 21 − 15 = 6 m north of the start, so √(8² + 6²) = 10 m to the north-east.

questions.stem: If south-east is called north, north-east is called west, and every other direction is renamed in the same way, what is west called?
questions.explanation: Each direction is turned 135° anticlockwise: south-east to north, north-east to west. Turning west 135° anticlockwise gives south-east.

questions.stem: Neha is 11th from the top and 27th from the bottom in her class. How many students are in the class?
questions.explanation: Total = 11 + 27 − 1 = 37, because Neha is counted in both positions.

questions.stem: How many letters lie between the 9th letter from the left and the 4th letter from the right in the English alphabet?
questions.explanation: The 9th letter from the left is I and the 4th from the right is W (23rd). Between them are 23 − 9 − 1 = 13 letters.

questions.stem: What do business correspondents do, according to the passage?
options: Lend money from their own savings
Offer basic banking for a bank locally
Sell shop goods on credit to farmers
Run bus services to bank branches
questions.explanation: The passage says they open accounts, accept deposits and pay out withdrawals on behalf of a bank, near where people live.

questions.stem: Why do some agents drift away to other work?
options: The devices are too hard to use
Banks forbid them to run shops
questions.explanation: The passage says that where commissions are thin, agents drift away to other work.

questions.stem: What change have some banks made to keep their agents?
options: A rule that agents cannot quit
A fixed monthly sum plus commission
questions.explanation: Some banks pay agents a small fixed amount each month as well as a commission, so a quiet month does not drive them out.

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly the SAME in meaning as 'thin' as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: 'Where commissions are thin' means they are meagre, too small. Slender and watery are other senses of thin that describe objects and liquids.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that fits the blank to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful.

The loan was ........ only after the borrower submitted proof of income.
questions.explanation: A bank sanctions, or approves, a loan once it has proof of income. A loan is not repaid before it is given.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that fits the blank to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful.

Small savings, made ........, can grow into a large sum over many years.
questions.explanation: Savings grow over many years when they are made regularly, month after month.

questions.stem:
Choose the pair of words that fits the two blanks, in order, to make the sentence meaningful.

The ........ of the new branch was ........ by a power cut on the opening day.
questions.explanation: A power cut on the opening day delays a launch. 'Launched, delay' and 'delay, launched' put the wrong parts of speech in the blanks.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence and find the part that contains an error. If there is no error, choose E.

The teacher, as well as (A) / the students, (B) / were present (C) / at the function. (D) / No error (E)
questions.explanation: A phrase added with 'as well as' does not change the subject. 'The teacher' is singular, so the verb is 'was present'.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence and find the part that contains an error. If there is no error, choose E.

Scarcely had we (A) / sat down for dinner (B) / when the lights (C) / went out. (D) / No error (E)
questions.explanation: The sentence is correct: 'scarcely' takes inverted word order and 'when'.

questions.stem:
Which of the following should replace the part in bold to make the sentence correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No improvement'.

She is **too much tired** to walk any further.
questions.explanation: Before an adjective, 'too' is used alone: 'too tired to walk'. 'Much' does not go with 'tired' here.

questions.stem:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following question?

7/12 of 1,080 − 35% of 600 = ?
questions.explanation: 7/12 of 1,080 = 630 and 35% of 600 = 210, so the answer is 420.

questions.stem:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following number series?

14, 17, 23, 32, 44, ?
questions.explanation: The differences are 3, 6, 9, 12, so the next difference is 15 and 44 + 15 = 59.

questions.stem:
Two equations, I and II, are given. Solve both and choose the correct relationship between x and y.

I. x² − 9 = 0

II. y² − 7y + 12 = 0
options: x = y or no relation can be established
questions.explanation: I: x = 3 or −3. II: y = 3 or 4. x = 3 equals y = 3 and is below 4, and x = −3 is below both. So x ≤ y.

questions.stem: What is the total area (in hectares) sown with wheat in the four villages?
The wheat area of Devgarh is how many times its mustard area?
What is the ratio of the total wheat area to the total mustard area of the four villages?
Sitapur's mustard area is what percentage of its wheat area?
Two successive discounts of 25% and 12% are equal to a single discount of:
questions.explanation: After 25% off, 75 remains; 12% off that leaves 66. The single discount is 34%, not 37%.

questions.stem: The sum of the present ages of a mother and her daughter is 56 years. Four years ago the mother was three times as old as the daughter. What is the daughter's present age in years?
questions.explanation: Let the daughter be d. Then 56 − d − 4 = 3(d − 4), so 52 − d = 3d − 12 and d = 16.

questions.stem: A cyclist rides to a village at 30 km/h and returns along the same road at 45 km/h. What is her average speed for the whole journey in km/h?
questions.explanation: For equal distances the average speed is 2 × 30 × 45 ÷ (30 + 45) = 36 km/h, not the simple average of 37.5.

questions.stem:

Statement: H < I = J ≥ K > L

I. H < J

II. L < I
questions.explanation: I: H < I = J gives H < J, true. II: I = J ≥ K > L gives I > L, true. Both follow.

questions.stem:
A statement is followed by two conclusions, I and II. Assume the statement is true and decide which conclusion(s) definitely follow.

Statement: C ≤ D < E ≥ F = G

I. C < F

II. G ≤ E
questions.explanation: I: D < E and E ≥ F point in opposite directions, so C and F cannot be compared. II: E ≥ F = G gives G ≤ E, true. Only II follows.

questions.stem:

Statements: All apples are fruits. No fruit is a stone.

I. No apple is a stone.

II. Some stones are apples.
questions.explanation: Every apple is a fruit and no fruit is a stone, so no apple is a stone (I). That makes II false. Only I follows.

questions.stem: On which day is A's meeting?
questions.explanation: Monday to Friday: C (Savings), E (Loans), A (Insurance), B (Pensions), D (Cards). D is Friday, so C and B, three days apart, are Monday and Thursday. E is just before A in the free days Tuesday and Wednesday, and C is before A, so C is Monday and B Thursday. Loans follows C's meeting; Insurance is not Monday, so it is Wednesday and Savings Monday.

questions.stem: Which topic does E's meeting cover?
questions.explanation: Monday to Friday: C (Savings), E (Loans), A (Insurance), B (Pensions), D (Cards). D is Friday, so C and B, three days apart, are Monday and Thursday. E is just before A in the free days Tuesday and Wednesday, and C is before A, so C is Monday and B Thursday. Loans follows C's meeting; Insurance is not Monday, so it is Wednesday and Savings Monday.

questions.stem: How many meetings are held between C's and D's meetings?
questions.explanation: Monday to Friday: C (Savings), E (Loans), A (Insurance), B (Pensions), D (Cards). D is Friday, so C and B, three days apart, are Monday and Thursday. E is just before A in the free days Tuesday and Wednesday, and C is before A, so C is Monday and B Thursday. Loans follows C's meeting; Insurance is not Monday, so it is Wednesday and Savings Monday.

questions.stem: Which topic is covered on Thursday?
questions.explanation: Monday to Friday: C (Savings), E (Loans), A (Insurance), B (Pensions), D (Cards). D is Friday, so C and B, three days apart, are Monday and Thursday. E is just before A in the free days Tuesday and Wednesday, and C is before A, so C is Monday and B Thursday. Loans follows C's meeting; Insurance is not Monday, so it is Wednesday and Savings Monday.

questions.stem: Whose meeting is on Savings?
questions.explanation: Monday to Friday: C (Savings), E (Loans), A (Insurance), B (Pensions), D (Cards). D is Friday, so C and B, three days apart, are Monday and Thursday. E is just before A in the free days Tuesday and Wednesday, and C is before A, so C is Monday and B Thursday. Loans follows C's meeting; Insurance is not Monday, so it is Wednesday and Savings Monday.

questions.stem: In a certain code, 'GOLD' is written as 'IQNF'. How is 'CASH' written in that code?
questions.explanation: Each letter moves two places forward: G→I, O→Q, L→N, D→F. So C→E, A→C, S→U, H→J, giving ECUJ.

questions.stem: K is the daughter of L. L is the brother of M. M is the mother of N. How is N related to K?
questions.explanation: L and M are brother and sister. K is L's child and N is M's child, so N is K's cousin.

questions.stem: In a queue, Raj is 12th from the front. Sita stands behind him with exactly 7 people between them, and she is 6th from the back. How many people are in the queue?
questions.explanation: Sita is 12 + 7 + 1 = 20th from the front. The total is 20 + 6 − 1 = 25.
